US hiring plans are picking up as seasonal demand accelerates:

US-based employers announced plans to hire 444,692 workers in October, up +57% YoY and the highest October total since at least 2009.

Technology led with 300,252 announced positions, followed by Transportation at 100,000, and Retail at 13,300.

Year-to-date hiring plans are up +34% YoY, to 655,304 workers.

Meanwhile, seasonal hiring announcements jumped +26% YoY, to 470,400, but remained 29% below the 660,150 recorded in 2024.

Seasonal positions now account for 72% of all hiring plans in 2026 and nearly 60% of the increase from last year.

Seasonal hiring is gaining momentum.

Serenity@aleabitoreddit
04:37 SGT quoteInvesting
Well, most of the time projections are noise and reactionary.

Like right now, sky-high projections for $ANT $700-$800B ARR over next few years is stirring up hype that I'd argue gets revised down later.

I do think it's important to model in capex forecasts dropping past 2028, due to the current reflexive nature of AI selloffs, rate hikes, etc.

The drawn out duration of Iran War doesn't help, Jensen leaving $NVDA certainty draws concerns over Nvidia's ecosystem.

But any catalyst, like if Iran War ends, can also change sentiment in a heartbeat (since bearish positioning is overwhelming).

- It's also clear financing has been tightening, since OpenAI only managed to raise $11B of their original $30B target so far.

- Markets are reacting enthusiastically to companies like $TE doing a $100M ATM today (nuking valuations)

- Although the "guppy" sector is probably the most sensitive to financing + rate changes.

On bright side... Neoclouds like $NBIS or $IREN seem to be adjusting by getting 100% capex prepayments or 90% GPU prepayments from their counterparties.

What I'd argue though is lower aggregate capex does not apply uniformly in supply chains.

- Mid-high range lasers for NPO/CPO are still sold out, as seen with $LITE now starting negotiations for 2030 capacity.
- MLCCs are seeing further tightening as content usage goes up for AI servers
- ABF substrates to InP substrates not really going anywhere.

If content per system goes up 10X-15X, capacity expands at 2-3X Y/Y, and capex drops 28%.

And content is so cheap that you can triple order and screw over competitors with wafer supply...

I'm pretty confident you'll see acceleration upstream in bottlenecks from optical components to substrates despite potential aggregate capex dropping.

Another rant is:

-I keep seeing this argument that "low P/E is a warning for cyclical that's going to crash" but these are just clown takes

Nobody seems to analyze duration scenarios like capacity expansion vs. content changes vs. demand. to actually see how long those earnings last.

If everyone seems to be exiting DDR2 lines, there's probably going be more tightness in 2027 despite consume demand weakening, even if it looks like it's low P/E.

- Also for concerns about CPO "delays", the same components like lasers are used for NPO. You'll still see 150-200mW NPO lasers or ELS NPO using the same 300–400+ mW lasers as CPO.

We'll just see acceleration with NPO as a bridge if CPO gets delayed and higher range lasers likely to remain in a severe shortage.

- Feels like markets have also completely discredited the merit of take/pay price floor LTAs as well that companies like SK Hynix to Samsung have.

If contractual agreements hold up, memory players look very undervalued.

TLDR:
- I think it's important to model in capex decreasing to numbers like -30% in hypothetical downside sceanrios.

Given AI profitability, it's clearly not sustainable for hyperscalers to aggregately increase capex $500B or $1T+ Y/Y, and that's never been a case I've argued.

- This is also not the same thing as demand destruction that markets are overreacting to now (which haven't happened yet).

- We can see demand revisions for GPUs, ASICs, and heavier cost parts of the supply chain, while acceleration increases elsewhere.

The nuances market miss by indiscriminately selling everything is going to present compelling opportunities when the dust settles. I think in the end institutions are probably going to end up owning more of the same names retail discovered early on.

Anyway, I think it's a good idea to try and survive until more earnings comes out.

Enterprise AI is entering a period of explosive growth.

The global enterprise AI market is now projected to grow from $31.5 billion in 2025 to a record $155.2 billion by 2030.

This represents a +393% increase in just 5 years, primarily driven by increased adoption of AI.

However, the next phase of this expansion will be more custom-tailored.

Companies are looking AI solutions tailored to their specific operations, with a growing emphasis on cost efficiency and control.

The AI Revolution is rapidly moving from experimentation to enterprise-wide implementation.
Yejin Choi @YejinChoinka · 17 Nov 2026, 01:01 SGT
Through my wonderful time at NVIDIA and Stanford, one question has kept me up at night:

Should the future of AI be monolithic or plural?

To answer this question, we’ve raised $110M to get started, backed by @MenloVentures, @MadronaVentures, @NVIDIA, @NEA, @KindredVentures,@Wing_VC, @aixventureshq, @Cisco, @Snowflake, among others.

Today, Carlos (@guestrin) and I are stoked to launch Noeri, a neolab to push the frontier of plural intelligence.

Noeri means “the plural of intelligence” or many intelligences.

The future of AI we root for is plural: a healthy ecosystem of many intelligences, in all sizes, strengths, and quirks.

Discovery, in particular, has always been plural: many curious minds, each devoted to their own question, often on roads less traveled.

Our path there is self-improving AI that:

-> learns continually on the job, closing the gap between what AI can do off the shelf and what the dynamic world demands

-> learns to use other AIs as tools and make new tools to overcome its own limitations

-> picks the right-sized model for your problem, at a fraction of the frontier cost

Then the power of intelligence, from the craftsmanship of making AI to ownership, can be in the hands of all.

@noeri_ai mission reflects who we are as the founding team. My career has been anything but linear, literally continual learning on the job. Carlos has devoted his career to building tools that empower people through AI.

We are all a bit contrarian, a bit adventurous, and above all, big believers in pluralism.

Join us to build this future together: noeri.ai

This marks a sharp reversal after growth stocks outperformed value by 31.2 percentage points in 2023, 19.0 percentage points in 2024, and 2.7 percentage points in 2025.

By comparison, during the 2022 bear market, value stocks outperformed growth by 21.6 percentage points.

This comes as the Russell 1000 Value Index is up +24.8% year-to-date, while the Russell 1000 Growth Index is down -2.9% over the same period.

Market dynamics are rapidly shifting.

I believe that only the highest quality AI stocks should be considered going forwards.

The easy money has been made.

Random AI shitcos went up >100% in weeks from Q1-Q2 due to the entire supply chain going through a broad re-rating off of depressed valuations. Most of that pricing-in has been done now, and those exponential moves up (mainly driven by sentiment) won't return any time soon barring any genuine catalysts. Macro is too unstable.

In my opinion, it makes sense to be a little more cautious after the July de-leveraging. In practise, that would be: concentrating tech allocations into the highest quality AI compounders, and diversifying outwards slightly into non-tech sectors...depending on individual risk tolerance. (I am still heavily in tech due to a high pain threshold).

In fact, I'm already hearing that institutions are favouring such an approach heading into Q4, with financials and healthcare stocks being bought up instead of U.S. and European AI microcaps. (European funds in particular are double-y cautious).

Time will tell whether or not this is longer-term / tactical positioning.

Fun story - IRENted a POETry book from the library and I saw a WOLF outside.

Over the last 2 years, retail sales have risen +$69 billion, or +10%.

Meanwhile, US consumer sentiment fell -1.8 points in early October, to 46.3, its 2nd-lowest in history.

Sentiment deteriorated most among lower-income consumers and those with smaller stock market portfolios.

The disconnect between what consumers think about the economy and how they spend is widening.

A lot of you were asking me where my $HIMS Longevity as a Service thesis was coming from

Naturally, management wasn’t talking about it

Here’s $HIMS Chief Medical Officer confirming this is what they’re up to
Anant Vinjamoori, MD @dranantmd · 16 Nov 2026, 04:30 SGT
Phase 1 of the longevity market is over.

Phase 1 was access arbitrage: sell a bigger lab panel or a trending molecule, and early adopters paid just to get in the door. Now access is commoditizing fast.

Phase 2 is when longevity becomes the baseline:

1. Raw data stops being a moat unless it changes a real clinical decision.
2. Starting a protocol is table stakes; proving that metabolism, strength, or sleep improved six months later is the product.
3. Static playbooks lose to learning systems where the 10,000th patient gets a smarter plan from what was measured across the first 9,999.

Monday at 12:00 PM PT, I'm on the HLTH Main Stage for "When Longevity Becomes the Baseline" with Dawn Mussallem, Naveen Jain, and Heather Landi.

If you're in Vegas this week, come join us.

The most interesting lesson Jensen Huang taught me

And gave PTSD to Google executives over from his leadership at $NVDA:

Was that if a critical material can be bought out for spare change eg. ~$400m (FY2028 Photonics-SOI revenue forecast for $SOI)

And trigger tens of billions in economic impact to competitors for not securing supply:

We're going to see game theory bottleneck supply procurement actually accelerate upstream through 2027, with or without him.

I see Morgan Stanley's list highlighting CCL, ABF, PCBs, optical module components as interesting.

However; I'd put it through my own narrower lens, especially focusing on smaller component cost chokepoints + bottlenecks that doesn't cost much to secure capacity over.

Deleveraging/negative sentiment is indiscriminately moving the theme up and down together, so hard to argue individual fundamentals at this point.

Reflecting on 2026, I also prob need to be more selective of companies entering 2027:

But there's going to be a lot of outsized opportunities in bottlenecks... as new architectures like NPO/CPO emerge across the ecosystem.

Guy @nosilverv · 10 Nov 2026, 18:30 SGT
Bunch of people losing their shit: how does he have the time to be Stripe's CEO AND read Brothers Karamazov?

Same people are surprised by how fast the most effective operators text back. I think all comes from the same place: short feedback loops, which build causal models.

If you act on ideas *fast* they don't stay as ideas long which means you get feedback on errors *fast*. This compounds over time and all your models become causal: they track the actual moving structures of the world. If you don't act on ideas fast they proliferate and become these big castles, these flights-of-fancy that might be barely tethered to reality.

05:44 SGTInvesting
Why a Stock Can Rally 20% and Still Be in a Stage 4 Downtrend

One of the biggest mistakes investors & traders make during market corrections is confusing a sharp rally with the beginning of a new uptrend.

A stock can decline 40%, rally 20%, and still remain in Stage 4.

Here's why these rallies often fail:

1. Declining Moving Averages
- The 30-week moving average (roughly equivalent to the 200-day SMA) is still pointing downward.
- A sharp rally into a declining moving average is often a countertrend move, not a sustainable uptrend.

2. Overhead Supply
Investors who bought at higher prices may use the recovery to exit near breakeven, creating selling pressure that limits the rally.

3. Lower Highs
- A stock can rally 20% and still fail below its previous swing high.
- As long as price continues making lower highs and lower lows, the broader downtrend remains intact.

4. No Constructive Base
Sustainable recoveries often require time to build a base.

A few things worth watching:
- Price stops making lower lows.
- Selling volume dries up during pullbacks.
- Weekly price action begins tightening.
- The 30-week moving average starts flattening.
- Relative strength improves.

So, what do I look for instead?

I prefer stocks that have completed their Stage 4 decline, established a constructive Stage 1 base, and are transitioning into Stage 2 with improving volume and relative strength.

My biggest takeaway:

You don't need to capture the first 20% of a recovery to generate meaningful returns.

Waiting for confirmation may mean missing the initial bounce, but it can also help avoid failed rallies and unnecessary losses.

The goal isn't to catch the exact bottom. It's to participate in the middle of a sustainable uptrend while managing risk.

Steve Yegge @Steve_Yegge · 15 Nov 2026, 02:27 SGT
I just finished talks about my software factories at two conferences. Afterwards a bunch of people came up and told me what they were surprised about. Here is a distillation of what people thought were hot takes from my two talks.

First hot take: I tell everyone to slow down. Most speakers go on about how fast they're going, but I strongly believe in pacing AI outputs to human speeds. I regularly tell AI-pilled CIOs and CTOs to chill: almost nobody is _actually_ going fast with AI. Engineering still moves at engineering speeds, and business moves even slower. The ones pushing too hard are starting to see downtime for it.

If you don't pace your AI to human speeds, everything starts breaking around you, even at small operations like my online video game. I only have about a dozen humans working with my factory, and only a few hundred active old-timer players in the community who get along well, and still, introducing AI has still been very rocky.

My agents have, at times, overwhelmed my players with features, my accountant with emails, my merge queue with tickets, and my machines with load. Agents have pissed off my admins, resulting in name-calling, they've made messes in the game, and they've launched broken OSS without permission. The list goes on.

I can get away with all this chaos because everyone involved in my operation is very forgiving. They're excited by the potential. But even so, I had to learn to slow down, real fast. And so that's what I preach.

Hot take #2: Should you buy a software factory? Do you even need one? No. You probably don't need one. Factories take an extraordinary amount of upkeep. They turn into garbage mountains unless you put a frightening amount of time and tokens into curating them. I had to burn my previous five factories down since it eventually became cheaper to rewrite them than to fix them. So I'm not out there advocating for software factories or swarms just yet. If you do want one, be aware that it is a significant commitment of both money and human leadership to keep one running.

Several people told me that I was the only one who stood up onstage, at either conference, and said Build, don't Buy. But my experience is that software factories grow to be highly bespoke to your domain. Mine is super tangled up with my game, and I think that's inevitable. Because the factory is not just building my product, it's supporting it too. It's a company in a box. And they're easy for Claude to build for you.

Third and arguably hottest take: Next year will have a lot of human/agent and agent/agent office drama, resulting from bringing in AI employees, and it will be gloriously funny, but also frustrating.

Many of you are already on this bandwagon, but everyone next year will have a personal chief-of-staff agent. Busy people, even hobbyists, will have whole entourages of helper agents. The hot take is that people will become so dependent on these little private entourages, that they'll bring them to work. Your people will talk to my people, etc. Whole protocols will emerge for private entourages negotiating work between humans, inside companies big and small.

Nearly all humans will wind up having to start working with AI employees next year, and it'll be the beginning of the biggest cultural change we've seen in a hundred years.

So that's the hot takes. Slow down. Only build a factory if you think you really need one. And focus on empowering yourself with your own agentic chief of staff (or team). Your entourage will define how you work with others, so start by perfecting how you work with them yourself.
